summary:
SOL is an AI-assisted web prototype that helps astronauts and ground medical teams review changes in movement and physical performance throughout a space mission.
Changes in gravity can affect balance, coordination and critical task performance. These effects make personal monitoring important for astronaut health and safety during long missions and transitions back to planetary gravity.
Our prototype combines local video pose estimation with individual profiles and imported movement and heart-rate observations. It compares measurements with personal references and highlights deviations for review. Astronauts receive simple summaries, while medical teams can examine detailed trends. Our proposed workflow spans pre-flight assessment, in-flight monitoring and post-flight recovery, with future work focused on sensor integration, validation and spaceflight ergonomics.
details:
SOL Project Details

Smart Astronaut Health and Movement Intelligence

SOL Team, Nablus   NASA Space Apps Challenge

How the project works

1  Establish a personal reference
Each astronaut has a profile containing movement observations with timestamps, mission phase, task, gravity environment and reference measurements. The proposed pre-flight assessment would establish baseline movement, balance, coordination and reaction performance alongside relevant health information.

2  Estimate movement from video
Users can enable a camera or upload a recording. AI-based pose estimation identifies visible body landmarks locally in the browser. The prototype calculates a two-dimensional shoulder-hip-knee angle and retains landmark confidence. Video processing stays on the device.

3  Compare observations in context
Review rules compare measurements with a supplied personal reference. Observations with insufficient confidence or missing reference data are excluded from movement comparisons. Repeated deviations can prompt review of the task, restraint setup or movement pattern. Medical interpretation requires additional evidence and professional assessment.

4  Present information to each user
The astronaut interface presents clear summaries and reminders. The ground-team interface provides detailed measurements, trends, flagged observations and data-source information. CSV import and export support the review workflow.

5  Follow performance across mission phases
The proposed workflow connects pre-flight baseline assessment, in-flight monitoring and post-flight recovery evaluation. Future integration would synchronize camera and wearable data. After return to Earth, repeated functional assessments would help clinicians evaluate recovery and rehabilitation needs.

 

Tools used

Artificial intelligence tools
We used AI tools to support project planning, coding assistance, debugging and refinement of project documentation.

AI-based computer vision
Pose-estimation models identify visible body landmarks and support local movement measurements within the prototype.

Web development technologies
React, JavaScript, HTML and CSS support the interactive interfaces, application logic and visual styling.

Development and build tools
Code-editing, package-management and local development tools support dependency installation, testing and application builds.

Data handling and functional testing
CSV files support structured data exchange. Automated JavaScript checks cover input validation, missing measurements and reference comparisons.

Scientific reference resources
NASA research and human-system standards inform the project background, proposed assessment workflow and future validation approach.

Our goals

Our immediate goal is to make personal movement observations easier to understand and review. We want astronauts to receive useful, simple feedback while giving medical teams access to the supporting evidence and context.

Our next goals are to integrate authorized wearable sensors, validate movement measurements against reference equipment and evaluate the usefulness of review thresholds. Clinical and spaceflight validation will determine whether SOL can reliably support earlier recognition of meaningful changes. NASA's SM-301 research gap reinforces the importance of validating sensorimotor countermeasures in flight. [2]

Our long-term goal is to use validated findings to inform spaceflight ergonomics, including workstation design, restraints and task procedures. This research would build on existing NASA human-system standards and help test adaptations for different gravity environments. [3]
